case_name: Eugenia Michaelidou Developments Ltd and Michael Tymvios v. Turkey
court: The European Court of Human Rights (Third Section)

facts.text: The case originated in an application (no. 16163/90) against the Republic of Turkey lodged with the European Commission of Human Rights by Eugenia Michaelidou Developments Ltd and Dr Michael Tymvios on 26 January 1990.

anchor.surface_text: 1.  The case originated in an application (no. 16163/90) against the Republic of Turkey lodged with the European Commission of Human Rights (“the Commission”) under former Article 25 of the Convention for the Protection of Human Rights and Fundamental Freedoms (“the Convention”) by a company registered in Cyprus, Eugenia Michaelidou Developments Ltd, and a Cypriot national, Dr Michael Tymvios, (“the applicants”), on 26 January 1990.

facts.text: The applicants alleged a violation of Articles 1, 8 and 14 of the Convention, Article 1 of Protocol No. 1 and Articles 2 and 3 of Protocol no. 4, claiming the respondent Government prevented them from access, use and enjoyment of their property in northern Cyprus.

anchor.surface_text: 3.  The applicants alleged a violation of Articles 1, 8 and 14 of the Convention, Article 1 of Protocol No. 1 and Articles 2 and 3 of Protocol no. 4. They maintained in this connection that the authorities of the respondent Government prevented them from having access to, use and enjoyment of their property situated in northern Cyprus.

facts.text: The first applicant is a private company incorporated under Cypriot law and registered in Nicosia on 3 July 1986, with one director and two shareholders; the second applicant is a Cypriot national of Greek-Cypriot origin, born in 1948, living in Nicosia, director and principal shareholder of the first applicant.

anchor.surface_text: 10.  The first applicant is a private company incorporated under Cypriot law and registered in Nicosia on 3 July 1986. It has one director and two shareholders. The second applicant is a Cypriot national of Greek-Cypriot origin, born in 1948 and living in Nicosia. He is the director of the first applicant and also its principal shareholder. The second shareholder of the company is the second applicant's wife.

facts.text: From incorporation until 28 November 1986, the second applicant owned 1,960 shares and his wife 40 shares; since 29 November 1986, the applicant owns 1,999 shares and his wife one share.

anchor.surface_text: From the date of the incorporation of the first applicant until 28 November 1986, the second applicant owned 1,960 shares and his wife 40 shares. However, since 29 November 1986 the applicant has been the owner of 1,999 shares and his wife the owner of one share.

facts.text: In April 1988 the first applicant became co-owner of substantial property by way of gift, situated in Tymvou village, northern district of Nicosia, in the Turkish Republic of Northern Cyprus (TRNC), consisting of 51 plots of land with specified registration numbers.

anchor.surface_text: 11.  In April 1988 the first applicant became the co-owner of a substantial amount of property by way of gift. The property is situated in the village of Tymvou, in the northern district of Nicosia, located in the “Turkish Republic of Northern Cyprus” (“TRNC”). It consists of 51 plots of land with registration numbers A174, A194, A195, B245, B121, B238, B321, E262, E266, E268, E279, E291, E292, F221, F222, F301, F308, F314, F318, G102, G162, G193, G246, G288, G298, G299, G407, G411, G414, G415, G418, H17, H18, H26, H76, H87, H90, H98, H109, H112, H117, H130, H136, H144, H179, J12, J13, J32, J38, J46 and J55.

facts.text: The first applicant owned the property in equal shares with another company registered in Nicosia; on 3 April 1996 both transferred their shares by way of gift to the second applicant, who became exclusive owner of the property from that date.

anchor.surface_text: 12.  The first applicant owned the property in equal shares with another company also registered in Nicosia. However, on 3 April 1996 the first applicant and the other co-owner transferred their shares in the above property by way of gift to the second applicant. As from 3 April 1996 the second applicant became the exclusive owner of that property.

issues.text: Whether the Government's preliminary objections of inadmissibility ratione temporis, ratione loci, ratione personae, manifestly ill-founded nature, and lack of victim status are well-founded.

issues.text: Whether the applicant's denial of access to and control, use and enjoyment of his property in northern Cyprus constitutes a violation of Article 1 of Protocol No. 1.

anchor.surface_text: The applicant contended that the continuous denial of access to his property in northern Cyprus and the ensuing loss of all control of it constituted a violation of Article 1 of Protocol No. 1, which reads as follows: “Every natural or legal person is entitled to the peaceful enjoyment of his possessions...

issues.text: Whether the acts of the “TRNC” authorities and Turkey's responsibility under the Convention engage liability for the interference with property rights.

anchor.surface_text: The Government reiterated that they could not be held liable under the Convention for the acts of the authorities of the “TRNC”. They further maintained that the applicant's claims to his property needed to be considered in the context of the political situation in Cyprus and the de facto state of affairs on the island.

issues.text: Whether the Government's justifications for the interference with property rights, including the need to rehouse displaced Turkish Cypriot refugees and ongoing intercommunal talks, are valid under Article 1 of Protocol No. 1.

anchor.surface_text: Furthermore, the respondent Government disagreed with the findings of the Court in its judgments in the Loizidou case (op. cit.). They maintained that those judgments should not be considered as precedent for the purposes of this application...

issues.text: Whether the applicant is a victim within the meaning of Article 34 of the Convention, considering the close identification between the company and the individual applicant.

anchor.surface_text: Concerning the applicants' alleged lack of victim status, the Court notes that the first applicant is a company incorporated under Cypriot law and between April 1988 and April 1996 was the registered co-owner of the property in question...

issues.text: Whether it is necessary to examine separately the complaint under Article 14 taken in conjunction with Article 1 of Protocol No. 1.

anchor.surface_text: The Court sees no reason in this case to depart from that approach. Bearing in mind its conclusion on the complaint under Article 1 of Protocol No. 1, it finds that it is not necessary to carry out a separate examination of the complaint under Article 14 combined with Article 1 of Protocol No. 1.

issues.text: Whether the applicant's complaint of unjustified interference with his right to respect for his home under Article 8 of the Convention requires examination.

anchor.surface_text: The Court notes that the applicant has not submitted any pleadings on this issue including on the issue of applicability. It considers therefore that it is not necessary to examine this complaint.

issues.text: Whether the applicant's separate complaint under Article 1 of the Convention adds anything to the breach established under Article 1 of Protocol No. 1.

anchor.surface_text: The Court has found the respondent Government to be in breach of Article 1 of Protocol No. 1. In so doing, it has reaffirmed Turkey's responsibility under the Convention for that breach under Article 1 of the Convention.

issues.text: Whether the question of just satisfaction under Article 41 of the Convention is ready for decision in respect of pecuniary and non-pecuniary damage.

anchor.surface_text: In the circumstances of the case, the Court considers that the question of the application of Article 41 in respect of pecuniary and non-pecuniary damage is not ready for decision. The question must accordingly be reserved and the subsequent procedure fixed with due regard to any agreement which might be reached.

issues.text: Whether the Government's preliminary objection of non-exhaustion of domestic remedies raised after the admissibility decision can be taken into account at this stage of the proceedings.

anchor.surface_text: Lastly, as regards the objection of non-exhaustion of domestic remedies raised by the Government in their letter of 2 July 2003 relating to the “Law on Compensation for Immovable Properties Located within the Boundaries of the Turkish Republic of Northern Cyprus”, the Court notes that this objection was raised after the application was declared admissible.

issues.text: Whether the Court should have re-examined the case in light of the new Law on Compensation for Immovable Properties before delivering its judgment.

anchor.surface_text: This legislation undoubtedly constitutes a major development of relevance to all applications raising similar problems to those raised in the Loizidou case. In my opinion, before delivering its judgment in the present case, the Court should have examined the new situation in the light of the new legislation and at least requested observations from the respondent Government...

issues.text: Whether the Court's refusal to reopen the admissibility decision and consider the Government's late preliminary objection of non-exhaustion of domestic remedies was an erroneous interpretation of the Convention.

anchor.surface_text: The Court held that, following the decision on the admissibility of the application, the preliminary objection of failure to exhaust domestic remedies could no longer be raised (see paragraph 22 of the judgment). That, to my mind, is an erroneous interpretation of the relevant provisions of the Convention.

issues.text: Whether the introduction of new legislation providing for compensation constitutes new information that the Court should consider at an advanced stage of proceedings.

anchor.surface_text: The introduction of new legislation providing for compensation constitutes, over and above a remedy in the strict sense, “new information” of the utmost importance and, as such, cannot be disregarded by the Court or interpreted in a way that is purely procedural.

arguments.claim: The Court considered the first applicant company and second applicant individual so closely identified that it would be artificial to regard each separately for victim status; considered violations from standpoint of second applicant alone.

anchor.surface_text: Concerning the applicants' alleged lack of victim status, the Court notes that the first applicant is a company incorporated under Cypriot law and between April 1988 and April 1996 was the registered co-owner of the property in question. However, the second applicant has enjoyed total control of the first applicant ever since its incorporation in 1986. In particular, from 3 July 1986 until 28 November 1986, he held all of the shares in the first applicant apart from forty shares, which were in his wife's name; from 29 November 1986 onwards he held all shares, apart from one, which was owned by his wife. After 3 April 1996 the ownership of the property was assigned to the second applicant. In the Court's opinion, both applicants are so closely identified with each other that it would be artificial to regard each as an applicant in its/his own right. In reality, the first applicant is the second applicant's company and the vehicle for his business projects. On that understanding, the Court will consider the alleged violations of the Convention from the standpoint of the second applicant alone (hereinafter “the applicant”), there being no doubt that he can be considered a “victim” within the meaning of Article 34 of the Convention, including in the period between April 1988 and April 1996 when he, through his company, was a co-owner of the property at issue.
